questions.question: What does the generalized Extreme Value Theorem guarantee for a continuous function $f\colon \boldsymbol{E}\to \mathbb{R}$ on a compact set $\boldsymbol{X}\subseteq \boldsymbol{E}$?
options: It attains both a maximum and a minimum on $\boldsymbol{X}$.
It is constant on $\boldsymbol{X}$.
It is differentiable at each point of the set $\boldsymbol{X}$.
It maps $\boldsymbol{X}$ onto all of $\mathbb{R}$.

questions.question: Let $f\colon\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}$ be continuous. On which set must $f$ attain a maximum?
options: $\{\boldsymbol{x}\colon x_1\ge0\}$
$\{\boldsymbol{x}\colon\|\boldsymbol{x}\|\le1\}$
$\{\boldsymbol{x}\colon\|\boldsymbol{x}\|<1\}$
$\mathbb{R}^n$

questions.question: Which example fits the hypotheses of the generalized Extreme Value Theorem?
options: $f(x)=\frac{1}{x}$ on the bounded, half-open interval $(0,1]$.
$f(x)=x$ on the closed half-line $[0,\infty)$.
$f(x,y)=x+y$ on the closed unit disc in $\mathbb{R}^2$.

questions.question: Why is compactness important in the generalized Extreme Value Theorem?
options: Without compactness, a continuous function may fail to attain extrema.
Without compactness, a continuous function can never attain a maximum.
Compactness ensures the extrema of $f$ lie on the boundary of the set.
Without compactness, a continuous function is always unbounded.

questions.question: What does the phrase 'attains its maximum' mean here?
options: There is some $\boldsymbol{x}\in\boldsymbol{X}$ such that $f(\boldsymbol{x})$ is the largest value of $f$ on $\boldsymbol{X}$.
The values $f(\boldsymbol{x})$, $\boldsymbol{x}\in\boldsymbol{X}$, are all bounded above by some real number.
There is some $\boldsymbol{x}\in\boldsymbol{X}$ where $f$ is larger than at all nearby points.
Some sequence $(\boldsymbol{x}_k)$ in $\boldsymbol{X}$ has $f(\boldsymbol{x}_k)$ converging to $\sup_{\boldsymbol{X}}f$.

questions.question: For $f(x)=\frac{1}{x}$ on $(0,1)$, does $f$ attain a maximum or minimum?
options: It has minimum $1$ but no maximum, since it blows up near $0$.
It is continuous but has no maximum and no minimum on $(0,1)$.
It is not continuous on $(0,1)$, because it is unbounded there.
It attains both, because $(0,1)$ is a bounded subset of $\mathbb{R}$.

questions.question: Together with the intermediate value theorem, what additional picture does the generalized Extreme Value Theorem give for a continuous function on a connected compact set?
options: The range is an open interval $(m,M)$ between infimum and supremum.
The range is a compact set, possibly with gaps between $m$ and $M$.
The domain must itself be a closed interval $[a,b]$ in $\mathbb{R}$.
The range is the closed interval $[m,M]$ from minimum to maximum.

questions.question: Which two hypotheses are central in the generalized Extreme Value Theorem?
options: Closedness of $\boldsymbol{X}$ and continuity of $f$ on $\boldsymbol{X}$.
Compactness of $\boldsymbol{X}$ and continuity of $f$ on $\boldsymbol{X}$.
Boundedness of $\boldsymbol{X}$ and continuity of $f$ on $\boldsymbol{X}$.
Connectedness of $\boldsymbol{X}$ and continuity of $f$ on $\boldsymbol{X}$.

questions.question: Let $f(x)=x^2$ on $[0,1]$. Which conclusion follows from the generalized Extreme Value Theorem?
options: $f$ attains its max and min inside $(0,1)$.
$f'(x)=0$ at both extreme points of $f$.
$f$ is bounded, but its max may not be attained.
$f$ attains its max and min on $[0,1]$.

questions.question: Why does $f(x)=1/x$ on $(0,1)$ fail to fit the compact-domain hypothesis?
options: $f$ is not continuous on $(0,1)$.
The interval $(0,1)$ is not compact.
The interval $(0,1)$ is not bounded.
The interval $(0,1)$ is not connected.

questions.question: If $f$ is continuous on compact non-empty $\boldsymbol{X}$, which statement is guaranteed?
options: $f$ attains its minimum and maximum on $\boldsymbol{X}$.
$f$ attains its extrema only at boundary points of $\boldsymbol{X}$.
$f$ takes every value between its minimum and maximum.
$f$ is bounded on $\boldsymbol{X}$, but need not attain its minimum.

questions.question: Let $f$ be continuous on a nonempty compact set $X\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n$, so $f$ attains its maximum at some $\boldsymbol{x}^*\in X$. What else does the theorem tell us about $\boldsymbol{x}^*$?
options: Nothing more: $\boldsymbol{x}^*$ exists, but need not be unique, interior, or a point where derivatives vanish.
$\boldsymbol{x}^*$ is the only point of $X$ at which $f$ takes its maximum value, so the maximiser is unique.
$\boldsymbol{x}^*$ is an interior point of $X$ at which the derivatives of $f$ are all equal to zero.
$\boldsymbol{x}^*$ lies on the boundary of $X$, where the function leaves the set in its direction of increase.
